answers.1i: AO2 (3 marks)/AO3 (3 marks). A PPC shows combinations of goods producible with available resources. At A, 350 million capital goods and 160 million consumer goods are produced; moving to B raises capital goods to 450 million but reduces consumer goods by 30 million to 130 million (opportunity cost). Increased capital-goods production can expand productive capacity, shift the PPC outwards and allow more capital and consumer goods in future; this is positive economic growth. Level guidance: 1–2 basic, limited application/analysis; 3–4 partial application and some analysis; 5–6 clear, appropriate application and thorough analysis.

answers.2g: AO2 (3 marks)/AO3 (3 marks)/AO4 (3 marks). AO2/AO3: division of labour breaks production into smaller tasks; each worker specialises (for example handling the screen, checking the phone or packaging it); specialisation can make work faster and more accurate, increasing productivity and reducing Foxconn’s production costs. Workers avoid time lost switching tasks. AO4: repetitive iPhone tasks may bore workers and reduce motivation, causing mistakes, rework, lower productivity and higher costs. A failure at one production stage can halt later stages; this risk may matter with 270,000 workers and many divided tasks. Specialisation may also create problems when a worker is absent and no replacement has the required skill. Level guidance: 1–3 basic/limited and one-sided; 4–6 partial analysis with more than one view but potentially unbalanced; 7–9 clear applied analysis and a balanced, coherent evaluation.

answers.3b: AO1 1 mark. The only correct answer is C, to close the income gap between the rich and the poor.

answers.3d: AO2 (3 marks)/AO3 (3 marks). External costs are negative impacts on third parties. Local people and workers in Sydney’s business district could experience noise and air pollution, congestion or overcrowding during construction of the $296m residential tower. Construction may create noise and dust and require many vehicles; the affected third parties are neither the producers nor consumers. Level guidance: 1–2 basic/limited; 3–4 partial application and some analysis; 5–6 clear application and thorough analysis.
answers.3e: AO2 (3 marks)/AO3 (3 marks)/AO4 (3 marks). AO2/AO3: migration is movement to live in a foreign country; migrant workers increase labour supply, potentially shifting labour supply right, increasing employment and reducing shortages. Dubai’s 2 million migrants (80% of the population), including construction workers, make a large contribution to labour supply and may support productivity and economic expansion. AO4: most migrants work in construction, cleaning and care, so other sectors may still lack workers; migrants may not have the required skills and supply may be short-term if they return home. Raising the retirement age, lowering the school-leaving age or enabling more women to work may offer a more effective long-term or cross-sector labour supply. Level guidance: 1–3 basic/limited and one-sided; 4–6 partial analysis and potentially unbalanced; 7–9 clear applied analysis and balanced evaluation.
answers.4a: AO2 2 marks. Select product X (inelastic PED); total revenue = $3,000 × 50 = $150,000. Award one mark for selecting X and one for correct revenue; award both for $150,000 without workings.
answers.4b: AO2 (3 marks)/AO3 (3 marks). Consumers may not calculate what is best for them; increased advertising can pressure them to buy unhealthy products. Consumers may lack full information about the negative effects of sugar in drinks such as Coca Cola and Fanta. Habits and taste can make behaviour difficult to change; consumers may continue buying despite the extra 0.50 zloty ($0.11) per litre, especially if it is a small share of income. Friends’ consumption may also influence consumers to copy the behaviour. Level guidance: 1–2 basic/limited; 3–4 partial application and some analysis; 5–6 clear application and thorough analysis.
answers.4c: AO2 (4 marks)/AO3 (4 marks)/AO4 (4 marks). AO2/AO3: expansion may serve more customers and increase profit; NT Massage could charge higher prices in busier locations, attract tourists and business people, increase revenue, spread risk beyond its current residential location, gain access to finance and benefit from economies of scale such as spreading advertising costs. AO4: expansion could weaken the traditional service valued by long-standing customers; coordinating several shops may create diseconomies of scale for a family used to one shop; competitors may make custom difficult to attract; growth takes time and money, delays profit and may strain the existing business. The judgement may depend on competitors, successful advertising and tourism/business demand. Level guidance: 1–4 isolated/basic, limited development, one-sided and unlikely supported judgement; 5–8 some selectivity and development, more than one view but balance/support may be limited; 9–12 specific, accurate, coherent applied analysis, balanced evaluation and supported judgement.

AO2 (4 marks)/AO3 (4 marks)/AO4 (4 marks)
AO2 and AO3
• The quantity of workers whom producers are willing and able to employ is known as the demand for labour
• It can be affected by demand for the product (derived demand), productivity and availability of substitutes, such as machines
• The greater the demand for a good or service, the greater the demand for labour is likely to be
• This means that more security staff are likely to be demanded to control spectators at sporting events or at music festivals because there is a greater demand from fans to watch the event
• As there is a greater demand for food from those celebrating special holidays, more supermarket staff are likely to be demanded to sell goods to these customers at certain times of the year
• Similarly, if there is less demand for a service, such as at a football stadium when no matches are being played, there will be less demand for labour, such as security staff
• As a result, the demand for labour is affected considerably by derived demand
AO4
• However, even with an increase in demand for some goods and services, machinery may be substituted to meet the additional demand
• This means that the demand for labour would not always increase due to derived demand
• It is also possible that employees may be more productive under certain circumstances, meaning they can meet additional demand for goods and services without there being an actual increase in the demand for labour
• At the same time, high levels of productivity may mean the firm requires fewer workers as costs can be reduced. This would again have a significant effect on the demand for labour
• The advancement of technology has seen labour being replaced by machines in many industries, such as hospitality and customer services, as well as manufacturing
• Although, the demand for labour is likely to increasingly be affected by the availability of substitutes. E.g. the availability of substitutes would be limited for security at music festivals and sporting events
• The significance of derived demand may depend on the industry, as some work may be conducted by machines instead
• It may also depend on the extent to which labour is needed to develop, build and maintain machines that have been used as substitutes for labour because this could reduce the effect this factor has on the demand for labour
Level | Mark | Descriptor
0 | 0 | No rewardable material.
Level 1 | 1–4 | Demonstrates isolated elements of relevant knowledge and understanding; may lack development of relevant points.
